items.displayTitle: What is Life All About?
items.author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
items.description: In this program Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that the world's biggest problem is neither war, disease nor poverty but that people do not know who they are, mistaking the body they see in a mirror for the self. He distinguishes body from soul, calls the body a garment worn for fifty or a hundred years, and observes that people feed the body three meals a day while giving the real person nothing, describing the soul as literally a piece of the breath God breathed into Adam and claiming it can grow to immense size when nourished. He says the nourishment is a specific method rather than vague spirituality or ordinary supplication: five daily contacts with God following what he compares to the numerical combination of a safe, with fasting as a further practice, and he offers newly obtained mathematically coded evidence as his authority. Citing the Barbara Hutton story and Eddie Murphy's interview with Barbara Walters as cases of wealth without happiness, he closes by inviting viewers to examine the physical evidence free of charge, giving an address on East 6th Street in Tucson and a telephone number.

items.author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that idol worship persists because people do not grasp the greatness of God, and devotes the sermon to establishing that scale from what he presents as established scientific facts. He works outward from the solar system, whose sunlight reaches Earth in four minutes and whose span runs to billions of miles, to the Milky Way, which light would take a hundred thousand years to cross, to a neighboring galaxy two million light years away, to a universe of a billion galaxies and a billion trillion stars measuring some 26 billion light years across, pausing to calculate that merely counting a quintillion stars at one per second would take 32 billion years. He then states, on the authority of the Quran and its mathematical code, that this universe is the smallest and innermost of seven, so that no number can express the circumference of the outermost, and cites Sura 39:67 on the heavens held in God's hand as an allegory for that greatness. He concludes that against this scale it is blasphemous to attribute to God a son, wife or mother, or to idolize Muhammad, Jesus, Mary or a saint, asking what role any of them played in setting the synchronized rotation of the moon or the precision of the orbits. Recording date: this is the Friday sermon of 4 August 1988. It was also uploaded separately as a dated Friday sermon, and that upload was the only place the date was stated; the two were proven to be one recording by a flat timestamp offset across sixteen minutes, so the duplicate entry was merged into this one and its dating carried over. This transcript is the fuller of the two, being the only one to include the opening takbirs from 00:01:19.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa narrates how he came to the Quran's mathematical code and then walks through the findings one by one with a printed Quran in hand. He recounts arriving in the United States in 1968, disliking every English translation he read, and beginning his own for his children with a pledge not to pass a verse until he understood it, which stopped him at the initials A.L.M. of Sura 2; finding no scholar who could explain them, he entered the whole Quran into a computer and after four years of counting found 19 binding all fourteen sets of initials. The body of the program presents the counts in sequence: nineteen letters in the opening verse, 114 chapters, the first revelation positioned above the last nineteen chapters with nineteen words and 76 letters, the four words of the Bismillah occurring 19, 2698, 57 and 114 times, the missing Bismillah of Sura 9 restored by an extra one in Sura 27 exactly nineteen chapters later whose numbers total 342, matching the count of words between them, 6346 verses in all, and 5263 verses between the first and last initials. He continues through the words for Quran, for God being one, and for the five pillars, then the individual initial groups, Q in Suras 50 and 42, N in Sura 68, Saad across three chapters, Ya Seen in Sura 36, the seven H.M. chapters totalling 2147, and the A.L.M. and A.L.R. groups. The program closes with his answer to why the number is 19: that it is the numerical value of the Arabic word for one, in the system where alphabet letters served as numerals before Arabic numbers existed.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that the Bible is the word of God but that human interference has injected contradictions which drive intelligent readers away from it. He opens with the discrepancy Carl Sagan notes on page 30 of Contact, between Matthew's 28 generations from David to Jesus and Luke's 43, and treats the deification of Jesus as the largest distortion, reading the cry from the cross in Matthew 27:46 as incompatible both with Jesus being God and with the doctrine that he came to die for sins. He reads at length from The Myth of God Incarnate, naming its seven contributing theologians and their posts at Cambridge, Oxford and Birmingham and their thesis that Jesus was a man approved by God, as in Acts 2:21, and that the incarnation is a poetic rather than a literal claim. Estimating that ninety percent of the printed Bible is divine truth which readers abandon on account of the remainder, he presents the Quran as a mathematically composed final edition with four functions: exposing the injected contradictions, confirming the Bible's genuine content, settling controversies such as the crucifixion, which he says was inflicted on Jesus' body after the soul had been raised, and confirming earlier miracles such as the parting of the Red Sea. He illustrates the crucifixion argument with the case of artificial-heart recipient Bill Schroeder and closes by giving his Tucson address and telephone number for questions.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa, a biochemist, examines the evolution-creation debate as it reached the Supreme Court in 1987, arguing that mathematics can settle which events are probable. He summarizes Darwin's proposal and the modifications science has since imposed on it, punctuated equilibrium replacing gradual evolution and the abandonment of Lamarck, and offers the navel orange as an instance of real evolution within a kind. He then develops a probability argument from five cubes yielding 120 permutations up to 84 cubes, where the chance of one specific arrangement is effectively zero, and applies it to the 30 billion nucleotides of the human genome, the complexity of the so-called simple cell, and the eye, asking what told the dragonfly to stop at 30,000 lenses. Turning to creation, he argues that a mathematically coded message would constitute proof, quotes Duane Gish conceding that creation cannot be tested, cites Rabbi Judah the Pious on nineteen occurrences in the morning prayer, and describes putting the Quran into a computer and finding 19 across the initialed chapters and the four words of the opening statement, noting the finding's mention in Scientific American in September 1981. He concludes that the document confirms life beginning in water and presents evolution as a divinely guided process still underway, so that science and religion need not conflict, while correcting popular creationist claims about the age of the Earth, Noah's ark and the extent of the flood, which he blames for Darwin's own loss of faith.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that his generation is uniquely fortunate because the mathematical composition of scripture supplies tangible proof for statements earlier generations could only take on faith, such as Moses' staff becoming a snake or Jesus reviving the dead. He reviews the evidence in ascending order, including the nineteen letters of the opening verse, the 114 chapters, the 57 occurrences of Q in each of the two Q-initialed chapters, and the 2147 H.M. letters across seven chapters, noting that a hostile reviewer has now conceded several of the counts while still calling them coincidence. The center of the sermon is a discovery he credits to Lisa: that between the first Quranic initial in Sura 2 and the last in Sura 68 the verses number 5263 and the chapters fall into nineteen alternating groups, that the word Allah occurs 57 times outside that span, and that the sura and verse numbers of those occurrences total 2432, while Sura 68 itself does not contain the word at all. He closes by reading Psalm 91, which he holds to be mathematically authenticated as well, and applies its promise of angelic protection to the believer's confidence that God controls every outcome.

Along the way he treats the contact prayer as the connection lost by the generations described in Sura 19, comparing it to a combination to a safe and to ropes that keep a person out of a sizzling pan. items.description: Speaking without prepared notes, Dr. Rashad Khalifa asks why believers should love God most, and answers by reconstructing an account in which unclassified creatures divided when Satan claimed he could be a god: those who accepted God's absolute authority without question became angels, Satan became a jinn, and those who agreed with him mentally became human beings. He says that when God offered these humans a second chance on Earth, the angels of Sura 2 asked whether God would place corrupters there, which he reads as a call to send them straight to Hell, and he finds parallel traces in Romans 3:23, Romans 6:23 and Hebrews 1:3. The second sermon argues that the human race remains bad enough to justify that judgment, pointing to mosques he says violate Sura 72:18 and churches that call Jesus God, and then explains why he believes two false verses in Sura 9 were allowed to stand for fourteen centuries: a proposal during Uthman's committee to add praise of the prophet, which he says Ali opposed, leading to fifty years of war, the killing of the prophet's family at Karbala, and Marwan burning the original copy. He closes with the retribution described in Sura 22:19-22, an account of a Los Angeles meeting where Muslim attendees attacked his presentation rather than a professor who had called the Quran a hallucination, and the point that summing the Quran's numbers leaves no room for disputes about letter counts.

items.description: Answering a question at a 1988 United Submitters International conference, Dr. Rashad Khalifa recounts an experience during his pilgrimage in Mecca. He says the meaning was explained to him four months before this conference as the fulfilment of Sura 3:81, the prophets affirming a pledge to support a messenger who would confirm their messages. He then argues from Sura 16:2 and from Sura 22:75, which he stresses is in the present tense, that God continues to choose messengers, that everyone present who calls people to worship God alone is a messenger and a witness under Sura 22:78, and that his own role differs only in being specific. The session closes with a telegram from Ahmad Deedat addressing him by an Arabic epithet he locates in Suras 38 and 54, and with questions about the prophecy in Suras 9 and 48 that the message will prevail, the nineteen words of Sura 110, and the message reaching Japan and Latin America.

items.description: Lori leads a study of Sura 65 (Al-Talaq, 10–12) and Sura 66 (Al-Tahreem, 1–12), analyzing human creation, marital duties, and prophetic fallibility. Discussing 65:10–11, she explains that humans possess sufficient intelligence to believe rather than totally disbelieving like jinns, and that messengers serve to lead existing believers out of darkness. Dr. Rashad Khalifa addresses divorce laws, explaining alimony provisions and nursing mother allowances in 65:6–7. He argues that evolution within species is a divinely guided scientific fact, contrasting it with Darwinian natural selection and atheist evolution. He asserts that six other uninhabited Earths exist to prove on the Day of Judgment that life did not randomly evolve from chemical conditions. After an unedited manuscript typo found by Poopak is addressed, a participant questions how divorce arbitration functions in practice; Dr. Khalifa states that Quranic guidelines rely on conscience and mutual consultation. Transitioning to 66:1–7, Lori highlights Muhammad's human fallibility and the rejection of prophetic idolization. Hamid raises concerns regarding how far parents should force children to observe Salat, prompting Dr. Khalifa and Lori to cite 20:132 on persistent exhortation without compulsion. Beth offers personal testimony about her upbringing, noting that forcing children breeds resentment. Concluding with 66:8–12, Lori discusses sincere repentance, the struggle against hypocrites, and how the wives of Noah, Lot, Pharaoh, and Mary disprove the doctrine of intercession. The session ends with two recitations of Al-Fatiha for group members.

items.description: Edip Yuksel leads a study of Sura 70 (Al-Ma'arij), opening with Dr. Rashad Khalifa citing Sura 26 regarding reading the Quran in non-native languages. Examining 70:19–34, Edip addresses the passive creation of human anxiety, while Khalifa recounts an anecdote about his father's teacher debating mullahs over worry and despondency. Edip shares a personal story of a Turkish printing mix-up between 29:45 and 39:45 after neglecting his contact prayers. items.description: Apamea Bashar leads the study of Sura 71 (Noah) and Sura 72 (Al-Jinn) on May 19, 1989. Khalifa identifies the Dead Sea as a remnant of Noah's flood, highlights the scientific distinction between the sun's direct light and the moon's reflective surface in 71:16—citing Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin—and argues from 71:25 that souls learn their ultimate fate at death. Khalifa asserts Sura 72 prophesies events at Masjid Tucson, pointing to four occurrences of the root Rashada and 19-based gematria. He explains jinn mechanics, claiming they travel light-years and referencing a 76-second space shuttle launch abort. Khalifa interrupts to instruct youth attendee Amir on chastity, defining it as abstaining from premarital contact. In a debate over 72:18, Rami, Edip, and Dr. Mahmoud Sabahi question whether prohibiting names beside God's applies strictly to Contact Prayer or to physical mosque premises, while Khalifa argues for dedicated prayer spaces free of non-divine names.

items.description: Behrouz delivers a Friday Khutba addressing congregational decorum and reverence for God's messenger, Dr. Rashad Khalifa, following a visitor's concern over how Khalifa was treated. Citing numerous verses including 6:8–9, 49:1–5, and 24:62, Behrouz argues that believers must refrain from arguing with the messenger, raising their voices, or addressing him by his first name during official sessions, drawing comparisons to President Bush and citing Sammy Khalifa's conduct. Following prayer, Dr. Mahmoud Sabahi objects to Behrouz's tone, comparing it to rigid religious establishments. During the subsequent Quran study, Khalifa addresses human rebelliousness using the parable of the heifer in Sura 2 and recent dress-code breaches under 7:31, prompting commentary from Laurie, Linda Baroni, and others on modesty. Edip Yuksel defends himself against claims of ego worship, citing his sacrifices in Turkey and quoting 2:269, 17:36, 49:12, 24:63, 60:12, and 3:159 to argue that obedience is conditional and discussion is permitted. A heated debate ensues regarding past discussions on God's omnipotence and whether God operates through angels, during which Edip accuses Behrouz of claiming God did not create hydrogen. Khalifa, Ahmad, and Martha explain God's physical system of using angels (3:59, 15:29, 21:91), warning that raising opinions above the messenger nullifies good works (49:2). Dr. Mahmoud Sabahi recites Sura 114 and 3:103–106 appealing for unity, while Ali defends Edip's right to speak. Khalifa cautions Edip against idolizing his opinion (39:65). Douglas quotes 39:18 and 58:10 on Satanic division, after which Khalifa leads recitation of Al-Fatiha. Apamea Bashar concludes by teaching 3:130–132 and 2:275 on usury.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa leads a study of Sura 7 (Al-A'raf), verses 12 through 27, examining Satan's refusal to prostrate, his dismissal from God's kingdom, and his request for respite to lead humans astray. Khalifa argues that Satan's rebellion demonstrates free choice among creatures and asserts that opponents of God's physical evidence in the Quran use falsehood to combat truth, citing 40:5. Study participants Atif, Ihsan Ramadan, and Edip Yüksel discuss a conference where a scholar argued the Quran was hallucinated by Muhammad and where a critic objected to numeric counts over geminate letters (shaddas). Khalifa and Ihsan recount an incident where Ihsan experienced a separation of soul and body during a hospitalization, perceiving a large figure identified as Abraham. This prompts a detailed discussion on the nature of Adam and Eve's bodies in Paradise, verse 7:22, whether their physical forms were in Heaven or on Earth, and how souls are assigned to bodies. Parivash Ettefagh shares a dream about the Shahada and verse 7:172, arguing that human souls bore witness to God's lordship prior to earthly existence, making "Ash-hadu Alla Elaha Ella Allah" an eyewitness testimony. The group reads 38:67-76 regarding the High Society feud and 67:2 on the creation of death and life. Atif relates a clinical out-of-body experience during dental surgery, leading Khalifa to discuss Jesus's crucifixion, the distinction between body, spirit, and soul, and his own scientific publication on carrot cloning in Nature. The conversation concludes with remarks on Stephen Hawking and the fine-tuned expansion of the universe.

items.author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
items.description: Two Friday sermons in one recording, 3 December and 10 December 1982. Dr. Rashad Khalifa leads a study circle and Friday meeting in Tucson, Arizona, opening with a discussion on Sura 2:151 and the distinction between Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages. He argues that disbelievers experience physical pain inflicted by angels during death, contrasting this with the peaceful transition granted to believers and martyrs. Addressing modern religious struggle, Khalifa contends that ideological battles have replaced physical warfare. Dean Mahmoud recites Al-Fatihah (1:1–7) before attendees engage in an extended technical debate regarding the spherical geometry of determining the Qibla direction from Tucson to Mecca using compass bearings, great circle routes, and Earth's axis. Following informal birthday greetings, Khalifa announces upcoming Arabic classes and shares hate mail calling him a "deviated luminary." Turning to Sura 2:164, he highlights divine design in feline hearing, human dental anatomy, swallowing reflexes, atmospheric wind patterns, and desert seed germination. He presents the precision of planetary orbits and 4-billion-light-year cosmic distances as proofs of God. Explicating Sura 2:165–167, Khalifa asserts that idols and venerated figures—including Jesus and Muhammad—will disown their followers on Judgment Day, rejecting claims of intercession and comparing the Quranic narrative to Matthew 7:23.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa delivers a Friday sermon in Tucson, Arizona, explaining the purpose of human creation and the command to worship God alone as stated in Sura 67:1-2. He shows a slide of Earth from space to emphasize cosmic scale and human insignificance, arguing that venerated figures such as Jesus, Abraham, and Muhammad were temporary earthly residents. Citing Suras 5:75, 21:8, and 25:7, 20, he notes that prophets required food and visited markets, critiquing Hadith regulations regarding ritual purity and hygiene. He references Sura 24:55 to affirm that monotheists receive earthly authority, sharing an account of a woman surviving a gunshot to the head to illustrate God's ultimate sovereignty over life and death. In the second sermon, he discusses letters from a supporter in India who abandoned Hadith, claims Egyptian contractor Uthman Ahmad Uthman published one million copies of his Arabic booklet, and announces post-Zikr Arabic classes. He addresses converts maintaining their birth names rather than adopting Arabic ones, recounting an Iranian girl named Sherry who felt alienated by Arabic names at the mosque, which prompts a debate with attendees over slave names and adoption rules. Following congregational prayer, Dean Mahmoud recites Sura 2:168-176 and critiques extra-Quranic food restrictions, including Hanafi bans on shellfish, Indian cow veneration, Southeast Asian Hadiths against cucumbers, and Chinese ancestor offerings. Khalifa concludes by outlining the four explicit Quranic food prohibitions, dismissing Hadith bans on footwear and soap ingredients, and answering questions on store-bought meat and blood sausages before attendees recite Sura 2:177 and 2:178-179.

items.author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa and his study circle discuss the Quranic laws of equivalence, capital punishment, wills, and inheritance. Analyzing Sura 2:178-179, Khalifa argues that the law of equivalence sets a maximum ceiling of one soul for one soul to prevent tribal cycles of revenge, presenting it as an excuse to spare lives through compensation. He illustrates this with an anecdote of a University of Arizona arsonist and a Texas lethal injection case where a prosecutor admitted the wrong man was executed. Dean Mahmoud references Sura 5:33-34 to argue that harsher punishments apply to societal corruption and war, rather than general civil offenses. Turning to Sura 2:180-182, Latifa reads the verses on dictating a will and shares a personal anecdote about her stepbrothers raiding her deceased stepmother's house. Khalifa shares a similar story about his wife's family to show how wills prevent familial hostility. Dean Mahmoud details inheritance distribution under Sura 4, arguing that a father cannot disinherit his daughter, and recounts a legal case from Cairo where a son who repeatedly failed to murder his father was still granted his inheritance share. Khalifa and Dean Mahmoud criticize sectarian Shafi'i laws in Southeast Asia that disinherit non-Muslim or adopted children, citing Sura 33:5 to argue that adopted children must be treated equally to biological offspring. Dean Mahmoud recounts a story from the Philippines of a wealthy Muslim who gifted his estate to his adopted Christian son while alive to circumvent hostile relatives. The session concludes with Khalifa leading the recitation of Al-Fatihah.

items.description: Dean Mahmoud delivers a discourse on the creation of Adam and the nature of human power, referencing Sura 2:31, 18:53, 34:34, and 2:286. He argues that Satan uses forgetfulness to sever mankind's recognition of God as the ultimate source of power, presenting prayer and Quranic revelation as essential tools to counter this inclination. Analogizing potentiality to iron heated by fire, he asserts that human attributes and body parts will testify on the Day of Judgment. Following the congregational prayer, Dean Mahmoud, Dr. Rashad Khalifa, and participants engage in Q&A regarding mystical philosophy and Quranic numerical patterns. Dr. Khalifa discusses Ahmed Deedat and rejects Baha'i claims concerning the number 19, arguing that Baha'is use the number superstitiously outside the Quranic framework. Dean Mahmoud recounts a 1977 trip to Algeria involving Minister Mouloud Kacem and restrictions on his travel to Mostaganem. Dr. Khalifa details his background, including his doctorate at UC Riverside and his two years as a science advisor to Muammar Gaddafi. He explains how Gaddafi's rejection of Hadith began after discovering that a public motto attributed as a Hadith was fabricated, while cautioning an attendee that Gaddafi has rendered Libya an oppressive prison state.

items.author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa leads a study on the Quranic verses regarding fasting in Sura 2, beginning with verses 183 to 187. He argues that fasting was originally decreed through Abraham and initially prohibited sexual intercourse for the entire month of Ramadan, a rule later relaxed in verse 187. He challenges the traditional belief that the Quran was revealed over 23 years, asserting instead that the entire text was placed into Muhammad's heart on the Night of Power, citing Suras 44, 53, and 97, while Gabriel merely supervised its gradual release. Dean Mahmoud and an unnamed man raise questions about how companions distinguished revelation from ordinary speech, prompting Khalifa to reject traditional accounts of Muhammad fainting or experiencing epileptic symptoms. He references the spelling of Becca with a "B" in Sura 3:96 as proof of divine preservation, arguing the mathematical structure would collapse with an "M." Khalifa also critiques Abul A'la Maududi's theory on the Quranic initials, noting they only appear in 29 chapters. Discussing the physical demands of fasting and the Fajr prayer, he explains that the Earth's tilted axis and shifting seasons are designed to test the believers' commitment. He compares the body to a wild horse that must be tamed by the soul, quoting the General Electric motto to emphasize spiritual progress. He concludes with an anecdote about a car accident in Tripoli, Libya, which disproved his own theory that God takes three to six months to answer prayers.

He explains the conversion of sins to credits in 25:70 upon repenting from idol worship, emphasizing continuous repentance. Finally, he outlines the rules of Hajj in 2:196-198, recounting a trip with his father, and addresses objections regarding the Ka'aba and Safa and Marwah as potential idol worship.

items.description: Rashad Khalifa delivers a Friday sermon at the Masjid Tucson focusing on the absolute requirement of sinlessness for entering Paradise. He outlines two methods for erasing sins: immediate repentance (tawbah) and paying for them through worldly trials, assigning a hypothetical ten-thousand-dollar price to adultery. He examines Suras 4:17-18 and 39:53, noting that Moses was forgiven for murder due to immediate repentance. Citing Suras 4:48 and 4:116, he identifies idol worship as the sole unforgivable offense, criticizing Christians for idolizing Jesus and Muslims for idolizing Muhammad. In his second sermon, Khalifa asserts that Arabic fluency is not required to understand the Quran, citing Sura 41:44 to argue that God reveals the message directly to sincere hearts. He condemns traditional reliance on Hadith, Sunnah, ijma, and qiyas, citing Suras 17:45-46, 6:112-113, 39:45, and 40:10-12 to support the doctrine of Quran alone. During the subsequent question-and-answer session, he rejects belief in the evil eye as idol worship, explains that death occurs only by divine decree, and addresses double rewards for converts. The recording ends with a study of Sura 2:196 and the rituals of Hajj and Umrah.

items.description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa leads a Qur'an study session on Sura 2 (Al-Baqarah), discussing verses 158 and 196 through 213, alongside study group attendees Dean Majul, Jahan, and Abib. Dr. Khalifa argues that visiting the Prophet's tomb constitutes idol worship, while clarifying rules for Hajj pilgrimage, including expiation fasting, commercial benefits during Hajj, and the symbolic stoning of Satan at Mina. He and Dean Majul address Abraham's sacrifice test, noting the Qur'an never states God commanded the killing of his son, and explain the seven universes. Attendees recite verses 204 through 213, prompting discussions on hypocrites with impressive rhetoric, sinful pride, and Satan tempting believers to add unauthorized steps to religious practices like ablution. Dr. Khalifa reflects on facing persecution for upholding the Qur'an alone. Following the discussion, Dean Majul delivers a Friday Khutba focusing on Adam's disobedience in Sura 20:115, asserting it stemmed from Satan-induced forgetfulness rather than malicious intent. Citing Suras 15:29, 32:9, 51:56, and 91:7-10, Majul explores the divine spirit breathed into humanity, defining soul growth as actualizing innate capacities to know God and practice compassion. He shares an Arabic proverb regarding six urgent matters, including immediate repentance, before concluding with Sura 2:152 and leading the Friday prayer.
